name: Fall of Singapore
info: Japanese forces under General Tomoyuki Yamashita crossed the Johor Strait and took Singapore from the British garrison under Lieutenant-General Arthur Percival, who surrendered on 15 February 1942 in the Second World War.

facts.date: 8 to 15 February 1942; Percival surrendered on the afternoon of 15 February, shortly after 17:15
facts.place: The island of Singapore, across the Johor Strait from the Malayan mainland, then a British possession (present-day Singapore)
facts.sides: Britain and its Commonwealth forces (British, Indian, Australian and local troops) under Lieutenant-General Arthur Percival, with about 85,000 men, 15,000 of them in supply, administrative or other non-combatant roles; the Empire of Japan under General Tomoyuki Yamashita, with just over 30,000 men from three divisions
facts.outcome: Percival surrendered unconditionally. About 80,000 troops became prisoners of war, joining the 50,000 taken in Malaya, and Japan held Singapore until the end of the war.

t: The Japanese crossed the strait where the Australians held an 11 mile (18 km) front, and the defenders, spread along the whole coast with no suitable reserve, could not hold the beachhead.

Yamashita later called his attack a bluff, saying he had 30,000 men, was outnumbered more than three to one and feared being forced into costly street fighting, while Percival's garrison was short of water, food and ammunition.
Churchill called the fall of Singapore the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British history, and the loss of the base severely undermined British prestige in Asia.
dyk: Before the main attack the Japanese fired 88,000 shells along the strait in 15 hours, yet Malaya Command did not take the bombardment as a prelude to a landing and ordered no counter-battery fire on the Japanese assembly areas.
ev: Britain begins to establish a naval base at Singapore after the Anglo-Japanese alliance lapses
The Japanese 25th Army invades Malaya and Thailand, and Japanese aircraft sink the battleship Prince of Wales and the battlecruiser Repulse
The last Commonwealth forces cross the causeway to Singapore on 31 January and engineers blow it up
On 8 February Japanese troops begin crossing the Johor Strait and land against the 22nd Australian Brigade
The Jurong Line collapses on 10 February and the Japanese take the Bukit Timah area the next day
On 15 February Percival surrenders to Yamashita at the Ford Motor Factory
Japan renames the city Syonan-to and murders thousands in the Sook Ching massacre
Yamashita is hanged in the Philippines after a war crimes trial that did not cover crimes in Malaya or Singapore

sections.background:
Britain built a naval base at Singapore after the Anglo-Japanese alliance lapsed in 1923, and the base became a key part of interwar defence planning for the region under the Singapore strategy. Financial constraints hampered construction, and by the time war broke out in the Pacific shifting circumstances had largely undermined the premises of the strategy. During 1940 and 1941 the Allies imposed a trade embargo on Japan in response to its campaigns in China and its occupation of French Indochina. Japanese oil reserves were being rapidly depleted, and in the latter half of 1941 Japan began preparing for war to seize vital resources if peaceful efforts to buy them failed.

The basic plan for taking Singapore was worked out in July 1940. When the German raider Atlantis captured the steamer Automedon in November 1940, its papers, which described the weakness of the Singapore base, were handed to the Japanese in December. The Japanese had also broken British Army codes, and in January 1941 they read a message from Singapore to London complaining of the weak state of Fortress Singapore. They first suspected a plant and accepted it only after checking it against the Automedon papers.

The Japanese 25th Army invaded Malaya from Indochina on 8 December 1941, almost at the same time as the attack on Pearl Harbor. British thinking held the Japanese to be inferior and the jungle to be impassable, and the Japanese repeatedly outflanked hasty defensive lines. On 31 January 1942 the last Commonwealth forces crossed the causeway to Singapore and engineers blew it up.
sections.forces:
Percival commanded 85,000 men, the equivalent on paper of just over four divisions, of whom 15,000 were employed in supply, administrative or other non-combatant roles. The infantry numbered 49 battalions: 21 Indian, 13 British, six Australian, four Indian States Forces, three Straits Settlements Volunteer Force and two Malayan. The newly arrived 18th Infantry Division was at full strength but lacked experience and training. The rest of the force was of mixed quality, and the Australian official historian Lionel Wigmore noted that only one Indian battalion was up to numerical strength. Losses on the mainland had also left a general shortage of equipment.

Yamashita had just over 30,000 men from three divisions, the Imperial Guards, the 5th and the 18th, with a light tank brigade in support. The Japanese were superior in close air support, armour, co-ordination, tactics and experience, and had gained air supremacy; by the invasion only ten Hurricanes remained at Kallang.

Percival gave Major-General Gordon Bennett's 8th Australian Division the west of the island, including the likely landing points, with a frontage of over 11 mi (18 km) and no serious fixed defences, while the freshest formation, the 18th Division, held the north-east. Percival guessed that the Japanese would land in the north-east, ignoring advice that the north-west was more likely, and the Japanese deliberately moved troops to encourage this. He had spread his forces thinly along the whole coast and kept no suitable reserve.
sections.course:
From 3 February the Japanese shelled the garrison, and air attacks intensified over five days. Shortly before 20:30 on 8 February the first wave of the 5th and 18th Divisions began crossing the strait. The main weight, about 13,000 men from 16 assault battalions, fell on the 22nd Australian Brigade, whose battalions numbered about 3,000 men with no significant reserve. During the first night 13,000 Japanese landed, and another 10,000 followed after first light. Darkness and vegetation let the Japanese bypass or surround Australian pockets, and by 01:00 they were well established.

On 9 February Percival sent reinforcements, the Imperial Guards attacked the 27th Australian Brigade, and the 27th withdrew from its position, a move Bennett said he had not authorised. The Allies lost the beaches west of the causeway, and Guards armour and artillery crossed unopposed. On 10 February the Jurong Line collapsed after commanders misread orders and withdrew, and on 11 February the Japanese destroyed two thirds of X Battalion, a hastily formed unit of reinforcements, and took the Bukit Timah area with the garrison's main food and fuel depots.

Yamashita called on Percival on 11 February to give up. On the night of 12 and 13 February the Allies fell back to a 28 mi (45 km) perimeter round Singapore City, where a million civilians crowded into a small area as bombing, shelling and fears for the water supply grew. On 15 February Percival held a conference at 09:30, judged a counter-attack impossible and surrendered shortly after 17:15.
sections.aftermath:
Under the terms hostilities ceased at 20:30, and Yamashita accepted full responsibility for the lives of the civilians. Nearly 85,000 British, Indian and Commonwealth troops were captured, in addition to losses earlier in Malaya, and about 5,000 men were killed or wounded, a majority of them Australian. Japanese casualties on the island were 1,713 to 1,714 killed and 2,772 to 3,378 wounded. About 7,000 civilians had died by 15 February, not counting hundreds killed in earlier raids. Bennett handed over his division and left by boat for Australia, which caused controversy.

On 14 February Japanese troops entered the Alexandra Barracks Hospital and killed up to 50 soldiers, some of them undergoing surgery, along with doctors and nurses. About 200 staff and patients who had been bound were marched to an industrial area, bayoneted if they fell, held overnight in small rooms without water and bayoneted the next morning; a few survived by pretending to be dead. Later the Japanese murdered thousands of civilians, mostly ethnic Chinese, in the Sook Ching massacre, and other communities were not spared.

The city was renamed Syonan-to. Prisoners were held at Changi, and thousands were shipped to forced labour on projects such as the Siam-Burma Death Railway and Sandakan airfield, many dying on the ships and in captivity. Of about 40,000 Indian personnel in Singapore, about 30,000 joined the Indian National Army, and about 7,000 fought in Burma, Kohima and Imphal.
sections.sources:
The Australian official historian Lionel Wigmore described the state of the garrison's battalions, and a survivor of the Alexandra Hospital killings, Private Arthur Haines of the Wiltshire Regiment, wrote a four-page account that his daughter sold at auction in 2008. Yamashita's own remark that the attack was a bluff, Lord Moran's account of Churchill's reaction and Churchill's cable to Wavell of 10 February also survive; the cable put Percival's force at over 100,000 men, against 85,000 for the garrison's strength.

Numbers differ between accounts: the prisoners taken on the island are put at about 80,000 or nearly 85,000, and Japanese losses there at 1,713 to 1,714 dead and 2,772 to 3,378 wounded. The total for the campaign in Malaya and Singapore is 130,000 Commonwealth prisoners against 9,824 Japanese casualties.

The causes of defeat are disputed. Bennett blamed Percival and the Indian troops, and a classified wartime report by Wavell released in 1992 blamed the Australians. John Coates called that report lacking in substance and argued that the real cause was the failure of the Singapore strategy. The Kappe Report found that at most two thirds of the Australian troops manned the final perimeter. Clifford Kinvig blamed Brigadier Maxwell, and Costello called Percival's concentration of the 22nd Brigade at the water's edge a serious mistake. Post-war analysis holds that a counter-attack on 15 February might have succeeded.
sections.legacy:
Churchill called the fall of Singapore the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British history. His physician Lord Moran wrote that it stupefied him and left a scar on his mind. Together with the fall of Hong Kong and the loss of the Prince of Wales and the Repulse, it severely undermined British prestige in Asia. Alan Warren writes that it shattered the British Empire's illusion of permanence and strength, and presaged the end of colonialism in the region after the war.

The Australian prime minister, John Curtin, compared the loss to the evacuation at Dunkirk and said that the fall of Singapore opened the Battle for Australia. Hitler is reported to have forbidden his foreign minister to issue a congratulatory communique, deeming the defeat a setback for the white race.

Commando raids against shipping in Singapore Harbour followed in Operation Jaywick in 1943 and Operation Rimau in 1944, and British, Indian and Australian forces re-occupied the island in September 1945 in Operation Tiderace. Yamashita was convicted by a US military commission and hanged on 23 February 1946, but not for the crimes of his troops in Malaya or Singapore. Since 1998 Singapore has observed Total Defence Day on 15 February, the anniversary of the surrender, and sirens have sounded at 6.20 p.m. since 2015.

summary: In February 1942 Japanese troops under Yamashita crossed the Johor Strait and, in a week of fighting, forced the surrender of Percival's much larger garrison on 15 February. About 80,000 men became prisoners, and Churchill called it the worst disaster in British military history.

notes: The article says the bombardment began at 23:00 on 8 February and ran 15 hours, but also that the first wave crossed shortly before 20:30 on 8 February; I gave no start time for the bombardment.
Prisoners: the lead says about 80,000 (joining 50,000 from Malaya), the casualties section nearly 85,000; both in the text.
INA: the lead says about 40,000 Indian soldiers joined; the subsequent-events section says about 30,000 of 40,000 joined. I used the latter.
The lead says about a million civilians were crammed into 1 per cent of the island; the narrative says a 3 mi (4.8 km) area. I gave neither area.
Churchill's cable puts Percival at over 100,000 men with a [sic] in the article; I mention it only in the sources section.
The surrender time shortly after 17:15 sits oddly with the sirens at 6.20 p.m. said to match the actual time of surrender; left as the article gives each.
'Thompson wrote ...' and 'According to another source, Taylor cracked' name no work; left out. The Sook Ching toll is given only as thousands.
Left out: Parit Sulong, Heenan's execution, air operations detail, the Pasir Panjang battle, Dutch Batam and Riau events.
ev entry 1942 (Syonan-to and Sook Ching): the article gives no date for the Sook Ching massacre beyond 'after the surrender'.
